policy_name: Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Part 3 of Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022)
issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada (Government bill sponsored by the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry)
regulatory_regime: Proposed federal regulation of high-impact AI systems in international and interprovincial trade and commerce (never enacted)
geo_constraints: Would have applied to regulated activities carried out in the course of international or interprovincial trade and commerce in Canada

locale_context.regulation: Proposed binding law (lapsed) · high-impact AI duties
locale_context.culture: Canadian rights-protective, bilingual (EN/FR) federal tradition, close to EU-style risk-based thinking.

key_dates.event: Bill C-27 (incl. AIDA as Part 3) introduced and read a first time in the House of Commons (44th Parliament, 1st Session)
Second reading completed; referred to the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology (INDU)
Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry submits proposed AIDA amendments to INDU (incl. defined classes of high-impact systems and general-purpose AI obligations); never adopted
Parliament prorogued; Bill C-27 (and AIDA) died on the Order Paper at committee stage
Privacy portion reintroduced separately as Bill C-36 (reported); no AI-specific successor bill tabled as of latest sources

version: First reading text, 16 June 2022 (with unadopted ministerial amendments proposed in 2023)
covered_entities: persons responsible for an AI system (designing, developing, making available for use, or managing its operation)
persons carrying out regulated activities (processing/making available data for AI; designing, developing, making available or managing AI systems)
covered_systems: high-impact systems (criteria to be set by regulation)
covered_activities: processing or making available data for use in AI systems
designing, developing or making available for use an AI system
managing the operations of an AI system
exceptions: products, services or activities under the direction or control of the Minister of National Defence, CSIS, CSE and other persons/entities designated by regulation for national security
conditions: Core obligations applied only to high-impact systems as defined in regulations not yet made
Regulated activity must be in the course of international or interprovincial trade and commerce
objective: Regulate international and interprovincial trade and commerce in AI systems by establishing common requirements for the design, development and use of AI systems, including measures to mitigate risks of harm and biased output, and prohibit conduct in relation to AI systems that may result in serious harm to individuals or their interests.
principles: mitigation of harm and biased output
parent_policy: Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022

related_policies.policy: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Treasury Board of Canada)
Consumer Privacy Protection Act (Part 1 of Bill C-27)

conflict_rule: Not in force. Would not have applied to federal government institutions or national-security bodies; would have operated alongside federal privacy law (CPPA in Part 1 of C-27) and provincial law.

sources_consulted: https://www.parl.ca/legisinfo/en/bill/44-1/c-27 (not reachable from this session; via search results)
record_provenance.notes: parl.ca and justice.gc.ca could not be fetched from this session, so the bill text was not accessed: all clauses are paraphrases (text_is_verbatim=false) of the first-reading text based on law-firm summaries and general knowledge; section numbers refer to AIDA as enacted by clause 39 of Bill C-27 and should be verified. Status: AIDA died on the Order Paper on prorogation, 6 January 2025 (Parliament later dissolved for the April 2025 election). Minister of AI and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon has said AIDA will not be revived as such, and that new AI legislation may follow; as of the latest sources found (Aug–Oct 2026) no successor AI bill had been tabled. A privacy bill (C-36) reportedly tabled June 2026 does not include an AI act (secondary sources; not verified on parl.ca). Second-reading and amendment dates are from general knowledge and secondary sources. Penalty figures: up to the greater of C$25M and 5% of gross global revenues for s.38/39 offences (per Blakes summary); administrative/regulatory offence maxima (C$10M / 3%) from general knowledge.

clauses.original_text: [Paraphrase — not official text] A person who is responsible for an artificial intelligence system must, in accordance with the regulations, assess whether it is a high-impact system.
clauses.actor: person responsible for an AI system
clauses.object: whether the AI system is a high-impact system
clauses.condition: in the course of international or interprovincial trade and commerce; criteria set by regulation
clauses.exception: federal institutions and national security bodies
clauses.purpose: trigger risk-based obligations for high-impact systems
clauses.interpretation_notes: Paraphrase closely following the reported first-reading wording; never in force. Ministerial amendments (2023) would have replaced this with defined classes of high-impact systems.

clauses.original_text: [Paraphrase — not official text] A person who is responsible for a high-impact system must, in accordance with the regulations, establish measures to identify, assess and mitigate the risks of harm or biased output that could result from the use of the system.
clauses.actor: person responsible for a high-impact system
clauses.action: establish measures to identify, assess and mitigate
clauses.object: risks of harm or biased output
clauses.requirement: implement risk identification, assessment and mitigation for high-impact AI
clauses.affected_asset: physical/psychological integrity, property and economic interests of individuals; equality
clauses.interpretation_notes: Paraphrase; s. 9 required monitoring of compliance with and effectiveness of these measures, s. 10 record-keeping. 'Biased output' was defined by reference to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act.

clauses.section: AIDA s. 11 (Publication of description — making available / managing operation)
clauses.original_text: [Paraphrase — not official text] A person who makes available for use, or who manages the operation of, a high-impact system must, in the time and manner that may be prescribed by regulation, publish on a publicly available website a plain-language description of the system that explains how it is intended to be (or is) used, the types of content it generates and the decisions, recommendations or predictions it makes, the mitigation measures established, and any other prescribed information.
clauses.actor: person making available or managing a high-impact system
clauses.requirement: publicly disclose a plain-language description of the high-impact system
clauses.affected_asset: public's ability to understand AI use
clauses.interpretation_notes: Paraphrase combining s. 11(1) and 11(2); list of required elements recalled from first-reading text, not verified.

clauses.original_text: [Paraphrase — not official text] A person who is responsible for a high-impact system must, in accordance with the regulations and as soon as feasible, notify the Minister if the use of the system results or is likely to result in material harm.
clauses.actor: person responsible for a high-impact system
clauses.object: material harm resulting or likely to result from use of the system
clauses.recipient: Minister (of Innovation, Science and Industry, as designated)
clauses.requirement: notify the Minister of actual or likely material harm as soon as feasible
clauses.condition: use results or is likely to result in material harm
clauses.affected_asset: individuals' safety, property and economic interests
clauses.interpretation_notes: Paraphrase; wording matches law-firm reproductions of the provision. 'Material harm' left to regulations.

clauses.section: AIDA s. 39 (Offence — making AI system available causing serious harm or fraud)
clauses.original_text: [Paraphrase — not official text] Every person commits an offence if the person (a) without lawful excuse and knowing that or being reckless as to whether the use of an artificial intelligence system is likely to cause serious physical or psychological harm to an individual or substantial damage to an individual's property, makes the system available for use and its use causes such harm or damage; or (b) with intent to defraud the public and to cause substantial economic loss to an individual, makes an AI system available for use and its use causes that loss.
clauses.action: make an AI system available for use
clauses.object: AI system likely to cause serious harm, or used to defraud
clauses.requirement: do not knowingly/recklessly make available AI causing serious harm, or AI used to defraud the public
clauses.condition: knowledge or recklessness as to serious harm (a), or intent to defraud (b), and harm/loss actually caused
clauses.purpose: criminal deterrence of seriously harmful AI deployment
clauses.affected_asset: physical and psychological integrity, property, economic interests of individuals
clauses.interpretation_notes: Paraphrase; per s. 40 (as summarized by Blakes), conviction on indictment could carry a fine up to the greater of C$25M and 5% of gross global revenues (organizations). Applied to all AI systems, not only high-impact ones.
